analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above $50 million at 2%, rising to 3% above $1 billion, with doubled rates to fund universal health coverage.
analysis.headline: Eleven Democratic senators introduced a tax on wealth above $50 million; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put an annual tax on the net worth of the very richest households: 2% on every dollar of wealth above $50 million and 3% above $1 billion. Wealthy people who renounce US citizenship would pay a 40% exit tax on their assets. The bill also authorizes $100 billion for IRS enforcement, taxpayer services, and systems modernization, requires the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers each year, and adds penalties for undervaluing assets. If Congress later passes a universal health insurance program that bars private duplicate coverage, the top rate would double to 6% to help pay for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers. The tax falls only on households with a net worth above $50 million — roughly the richest one-tenth of one percent — and revenue from it, along with stronger IRS enforcement, is intended to fund public priorities, including universal health coverage if that legislation ever passes. Honest small businesses and individual filers also gain from better-funded IRS taxpayer services and modernized systems.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only above a $50 million threshold: 2% on wealth above $50 million and 3% on wealth above $1 billion, so all but the very richest households pay nothing.
The bill authorizes $70 billion for IRS enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for business systems modernization over fiscal years 2027-2037.

The Treasury Secretary must audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers annually, and the bill creates new penalties for substantial undervaluation of assets, applying a 30-50% penalty when a claimed asset value is 65% or less of the correct value.

If Congress enacts a universal health insurance program that provides comprehensive coverage to all US residents and bars private duplicate coverage, the top rate rises to 6% on wealth above $1 billion to help finance it.
Wealthy people who renounce their citizenship would be taxed as if they sold their assets, at a 40% rate, on the day before expatriation.

analysis.who_pays: Households with net worth above $50 million, plus trusts and family entities holding their assets. Financial institutions and business entities would bear new reporting obligations on asset values. The bill also bars deducting the wealth tax from income taxes and includes anti-avoidance rules targeting assets moved into foreign corporations, partnerships, or trusts.

drawbacks.text: Valuing hard-to-price assets — private companies, art, trusts — is difficult and contentious; the bill gives the Treasury Secretary broad authority to set new formulaic valuation methods, which would spawn years of litigation and disputes over presumptive values.
The Constitutionality and administrative burden of a federal wealth tax is contested; several similar proposals in prior Congresses never advanced, partly over these concerns.

Wealth taxes abroad have sometimes prompted the very rich to move assets or residence; the bill responds with an expatriation tax and anti-avoidance rules, but enforcement against internationally mobile wealth remains hard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on the top sliver of households, and the bill anticipates the practical objections with funding for enforcement, expanded audits, and penalties for undervaluation. The genuine uncertainty is administrative: valuing private assets annually is a real challenge, and the Secretary's broad new valuation powers would be tested in court. On the other side, the revenue could fund services that reach far more people than the tax touches.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late March 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not acted on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 26, 2026 by Senator Warren with 10 Democratic cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and the action history shows no markup, hearing, vote, or floor action since.
All 11 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has joined.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the wealthiest households, who owe nothing while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2026 and recruited 10 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 10 Democratic senators (Duckworth, Hirono, Markey, Merkley, Schiff, Smith, Schatz, Van Hollen, Welch, Whitehouse)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by Republicans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in a Republican-controlled Finance Committee; no Republican support is on record.

industries.note: An annual 2% levy on wealth above $50 million and 3% above $1 billion, with a 40% exit tax for those renouncing citizenship. The bill is designed so no household below the threshold pays anything.

The bill imposes new reporting obligations on financial institutions and business entities and targets assets shifted into foreign corporations, partnerships, and trusts to avoid disclosure. Clients with over $50 million would face substantial new compliance and planning demands.

The bill attributes trust-held assets back to the wealthy individual who transferred them, and taxes nongrantor multibeneficiary trusts, limiting a common route for sheltering family wealth — while expressly exempting charitable trusts.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic sponsorship and referral to a Finance Committee controlled by the other party, the realistic path is that the bill sits without action, as previous versions of this proposal have. Its main near-term function is as a stated position; it could return in a future budget or tax debate only if Senate control or the politics of tax policy change.
